subject: Historia
title: Emigration from Sweden
sourceSummary: Why around 1.3 million Swedes emigrated between 1850 and 1930, what the journey to America was like and how life turned out there – plus what the emigration meant for Sweden and which sources tell us about it.
topics: the journey and life in America
the consequences of emigration for Sweden

questions.prompt: Roughly how many Swedes emigrated during the great emigration between 1850 and 1930?
questions.opener: Sweden had around five million inhabitants in 1900 – the emigrants made up a large share of that.
questions.explanation: Around 1.3 million Swedes left the country during this period, which amounted to almost a quarter of the population – in some parishes in Småland and on Öland, a large share of the young people disappeared. Figures like 50,000 or 200,000 are far too low to explain why emigration became one of the biggest social issues of the time.

questions.topic: the journey and life in America
questions.prompt: Which country did most Swedish emigrants travel to?
questions.opener: Think about which country attracted people with "free land" in the mid-1800s.
questions.explanation: The great majority of Swedish emigrants travelled to the USA, where farmland and industrial jobs were the draw. A smaller number went to Canada and a few to South America or Australia, but they made up only a small proportion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a clear example of a push factor behind the emigration from Sweden?
questions.opener: A push factor pushes people away from their home country.
choices: The crop failures and famine during the crisis years of the late 1860s
The promise of cheap land in the Midwest
Letters from relatives who were already doing well in America
Cheap steamship tickets across the Atlantic
questions.explanation: Crop failure and starvation, as during the crisis years of 1867–1869, land shortage, poverty, harsh class divisions and the requirement to belong to the state church were push factors that drove people away from Sweden. Cheap land, enticing letters and cheap tickets were instead pull factors that drew people to America.

questions.prompt: Which American law from 1862 attracted many Swedes with the chance to get land of their own?
questions.opener: The law's name roughly means "the homestead law".
questions.explanation: The Homestead Act gave settlers the right to a plot of government land almost free of charge if they farmed it for a few years, which was enormously appealing to landless Swedes. The Monroe Doctrine concerned US foreign policy, the Bill of Rights concerned civil rights, and the Marshall Plan concerned aid to Europe after 1945.

questions.topic: the journey and life in America
questions.prompt: In which part of the USA did especially many Swedish emigrants settle?
questions.opener: The climate and forests there resembled the home country.
choices: The southern USA, such as Alabama and Georgia
The southwestern USA, such as Arizona and New Mexico
The Midwest, for example Minnesota, Illinois and Iowa
questions.explanation: Swedes headed above all to the Midwest, where farmland was cheap and the climate resembled Sweden's; Chicago became for a time one of the world's "most Swedish" cities. The southern USA and the southwest attracted few Swedes, and Alaska was in practice not a destination at all.

questions.prompt: Why are parish registers and household examination records such important sources when researching emigration?
questions.opener: Think about who kept records of the population before there was a tax agency.
choices: They contain photographs of every emigrant
Parish priests systematically recorded who was born, married, died and moved out of the parish
They describe what the emigrants felt and thought about the journey
They contain American authorities' decisions on immigration
questions.explanation: The parish priest kept careful records, and the out-migration registers list name, age, occupation and destination – which is why researchers can count and trace emigrants person by person. Feelings and experiences are instead found in letters and diaries, and photographs are rare in parish registers.

questions.topic: the consequences of emigration for Sweden
questions.prompt: Explain how the great emigration affected Sweden.
questions.opener: Think both about what was lost from the country and about what the emigration set in motion at home.
questions.answer: The emigration affected Sweden in several ways. In purely demographic terms, the country lost around 1.3 million people, mostly young people of working age, which meant the population grew more slowly and some rural parishes were emptied out. In the short term, pressure on the land and unemployment fell, and money sent home by emigrants helped many families. Politically, the emigration became an alarm signal: a state emigration inquiry was set up in 1907, and both conservative and liberal forces argued that Sweden had to become a country worth staying in. This strengthened demands for the right to vote, better housing, smallholdings of one's own, higher wages and social reforms. Culturally, strong ties were created across the Atlantic through letters, visits and Swedish-American newspapers and associations.
steps: Population loss: around 1.3 million emigrants, above all young people of working age.
The countryside was hit hardest – in some parishes a large share of the young people disappeared and farms were abandoned.
In the short term, competition for land and work eased, and money sent home strengthened the families who remained.
Politically, Sweden reacted: the 1907 emigration inquiry and demands for the right to vote, smallholdings and social reforms so that people would want to stay.
In the long term, lasting ties to the USA emerged through letters, returnees, associations and Swedish-American culture.

questions.prompt: Summarise Swedish emigration: scale, causes, journey, life and consequences.
questions.opener: Think about numbers, push and pull, the travel route, life in America and the effects at home.
questions.answer: About 1.3 million Swedes emigrated between 1850 and 1930, most to the USA · peaks around the crisis years of 1867–1869 and during the 1880s · push factors: land shortage as the population grew, poverty, crop failure and starvation, harsh class divisions, the requirement to belong to the state church, military service and a lack of future prospects · pull factors: the Homestead Act of 1862 with almost free land, jobs in American industry, religious freedom, cheap steamship tickets, agents' advertising and "America letters" from relatives · the journey often went Gothenburg–Hull–Liverpool–New York, later directly by steamship, and took one to three weeks in cramped conditions · many settled in the Midwest (Minnesota, Illinois, Iowa) as settlers, others worked in cities such as Chicago · Swedish-Americans built churches, associations and newspapers and kept the language alive for generations · consequences for Sweden: slower population growth, a depopulated countryside, money sent home, the 1907 emigration inquiry and strengthened demands for the right to vote, smallholdings and social reforms · sources: parish registers' out-migration records and passenger lists provide numbers, while letters, diaries and photographs tell of experiences – though letters can be one-sided since people were reluctant to write about failures.
